entities.name: John de Mowbray, 4th Baron Mowbray
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John de Mowbray, 4th Baron Mowbray (died 1368), was a prominent English nobleman and military figure whose life intersected with the tumultuous Anglo-French conflicts of the mid-14th century and the waning ideals of crusading chivalry. As a descendant of a powerful baronial family, his career was marked by military service during the early phases of the Hundred Years' War and his ultimate demise on a pilgrimage-crusade, reflecting the complex political and religious currents of the late medieval period. His lineage and lands placed him at the heart of English aristocratic power structures, directly involved in the martial and diplomatic endeavors of Edward III's reign.

Mowbray inherited his barony in 1327 and was summoned to Parliament from 1327 until his death. He actively participated in Edward III's campaigns in France, notably fighting at the Battle of Crécy in 1346, a pivotal English victory that showcased the effectiveness of the English longbow. He also served in the Scottish Marches, defending England's northern border against incursions. Towards the end of his life, Mowbray embarked on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, a common act of piety for medieval nobles. However, while passing through the Byzantine Empire, he was ambushed and killed by Turks near Constantinople in 1368, a tragic end for a man who had survived major European battles.

Mowbray's untimely death without issue would have been a significant blow to the family, but he had a son, John de Mowbray, 1st Earl of Nottingham, who succeeded him as 5th Baron Mowbray. This lineage continued to be a powerful force in English politics, culminating in the elevation of the Mowbrays to the Dukedom of Norfolk, thereby shaping the course of English aristocracy for centuries. His participation in the Hundred Years' War, particularly at Crécy, links him directly to the military innovations and shifting power dynamics that defined Anglo-French relations for over a century.

His participation in key battles like Crécy and his lineage contributed to the continuity of a powerful aristocratic family.
